methods.label: Compute the marked length and check the intersection choices
methods.explanation:
First assume that \(B'\) and \(C'\) mean the outer intersections marked in the figure. Equal radii place each intersection on the perpendicular bisector of the corresponding segment between centers. This makes a symmetric coordinate system useful.

[Figure 1](figures/1979_AMC_12_Q28_question_fig1.svg)

Since the three center distances are \(2\), triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral. Place
\[
A=(0,\sqrt3),\qquad B=(1,0),\qquad C=(-1,0).
\]
Its altitude is \(\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3\). Let
\[
h=\sqrt{r^2-1}.
\]
Here \(0<h<\sqrt3\), since \(1<r<2\). Each intersection of circles \(A\) and \(C\) is at distance \(h\) from the midpoint of \(AC\): a right triangle has hypotenuse \(r\) and other leg \(AC/2=1\).

The perpendicular bisector of \(AC\) makes an angle of \(30^\circ\) with a horizontal line. Thus a displacement of length \(h\) along it has vertical component \(h/2\) and horizontal component \(\sqrt3h/2\), by the \(30^\circ\) right-triangle property and the Pythagorean theorem. Reflecting across the vertical axis gives the corresponding construction for circles \(A\) and \(B\). The marked outer intersections are therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
B'&=\left(-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3h}{2},
\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac h2\right),\\
C'&=\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3h}{2},
\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac h2\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Their vertical coordinates agree, so their distance is the difference of their horizontal coordinates:
\[
B'C'=1+\sqrt3h
=\boxed{1+\sqrt{3(r^2-1)}}.
\]
Thus the marked outer intersections give choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

There is a qualification in the wording: being outside the third circle does not always select just one intersection. To check all possibilities, write the two intersections of circles \(A\) and \(C\) as
\[
U_\sigma=\left(-\frac12-\sigma\frac{\sqrt3h}{2},
\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\sigma\frac h2\right),
\qquad \sigma\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
The sign \(1\) selects the outer point and \(-1\) the other point. Their squared distances from \(B\) satisfy
\[
BU_\sigma^2-r^2=2+2\sigma\sqrt3h.
\]
The outer point is always outside circle \(B\). The other point is also outside exactly when \(h<1/\sqrt3\), equivalently \(r<2/\sqrt3\). The same calculation applies to the intersections of circles \(A\) and \(B\) relative to circle \(C\).

Consequently, when \(1<r<2/\sqrt3\), either intersection is allowed for each named point. Choosing both outer points gives \(1+\sqrt3h\); choosing both other points gives \(1-\sqrt3h\), which is positive in this range. Choosing one of each gives horizontal separation \(1\) and vertical separation \(h\), hence distance \(\sqrt{1+h^2}=r\). These four point-pair choices exhaust the possibilities, and the two mixed choices have the same length.

At \(r=2/\sqrt3\), the other intersections lie on the third circles, so they are not outside. For \(2/\sqrt3<r<2\), they lie inside. Thus D is uniquely determined by the written condition for \(2/\sqrt3\leq r<2\), and by the marked outer-intersection interpretation throughout \(1<r<2\). Over the entire stated interval, the wording alone has no unique answer.
